About this citation

Several letters quote an earlier author — Cleanthes, Hecato, Epicurus — and in those the quoted sentence is that author's, delivered in Seneca's Latin. The archive records the inner attribution in the source field where it is known.

#### About Seneca

Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE–65 CE) was a Cordoban-born Stoic, tragic playwright, and adviser—later forced suicide victim—under Nero.

### Interpretation

Seneca is quoting the Stoic teacher Hecato, and the sentence is a recommendation rather than an observation about reciprocity. His argument in the letter is that affection is not obtained by calculation or by obligation, but by being affectionate — so the usual strategy of trying to secure love is self-defeating. The claim rests on the Stoic view that what is up to us is our own conduct, not another person's response.

#### Why it matters

It is a correction to a common approach: trying to make someone love you through strategy fails for structural reasons. What is available is your own conduct.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “If you wish to be loved, love.”?

“If you wish to be loved, love.” comes from Letters to Lucilius, Ep. 9.6 (quoting Hecato) (c. 62–65 CE), attributed to Seneca.

#### What does Seneca mean by love?

Greek distinctions among eros, philia, and agape, Confucian relational ethics, and modern debates about romantic love keep the theme philosophically precise rather than merely sentimental. This passage enters that discussion through love, action.
